title: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
summary: How RDMA lets a NIC read and write remote memory: queue pairs and completions, memory registration and keys, one-sided versus two-sided verbs, InfiniBand vs RoCEv2 vs iWARP, and what limits it at scale.
outcomes: Explain which per-message costs of TCP sockets RDMA removes and why the kernel stays on the control path
Trace a work request from ibv_post_send through doorbell, execution and completion, and spot buffer-reuse bugs
Compute how a NIC resolves a remote address through a registration, and why huge pages shrink its translation table
Choose between SEND/RECV, RDMA WRITE, READ and atomics, and between RC, UC and UD, for a given design
Explain why RoCEv2 needs a lossless fabric, how PFC causes victim flows, and how DCQCN and tuning limits help

lessons.title: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes

blocks.md:
In the zero-copy I/O course you removed user-to-kernel copies with tools like `sendfile` and `splice`. The kernel is still on the data path, though: every send and receive is a system call, the TCP stack runs on a host CPU for every packet, and the receiver usually takes an interrupt and copies bytes out of a kernel buffer into the application's buffer.

NVIDIA's RDMA programming manual puts it bluntly: TCP/IP *requires operating system intervention for every operation*, including buffer copying on both ends, and because TCP is a byte stream the message boundaries are lost on the way.

**Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA)** changes who does the work. The operating system is used once, to *set up a channel*: create the queues, register memory, connect to the peer. After that the application hands work straight to the network card, and the card runs the transport protocol (segmentation, acknowledgements, retransmission) in hardware and places the data directly into the destination application's memory.

Two words you will see everywhere:

- **Kernel bypass**: the data path (posting work, collecting results) does not enter the kernel.
- **HCA** (host channel adapter) or **RNIC**: an RDMA-capable network card. The InfiniBand name is HCA; this course just says NIC.

blocks.title: Who touches a message: TCP versus RDMA

scenes.caption: Sockets: App A makes a system call, the kernel runs TCP and copies or pins the data, then the NIC sends it. Every message crosses the kernel twice, once per host.
RDMA data path: App A writes a work request the NIC reads directly. NIC B places the bytes in App B's registered buffer by DMA. Neither kernel runs per message.
The kernel did not disappear: it ran the control path earlier (open device, register memory, create and connect queues). After setup it is off the data path.

blocks.md: How much does this buy? Microsoft and Mellanox measured it on 40 Gbps NICs when deploying RDMA (the DCQCN paper, SIGCOMM 2015). With connections pre-established, warmed up and Nagle disabled, transferring a 2 KB message took 25.4 µs over TCP, 2.8 µs with RDMA SEND and 1.7 µs with RDMA READ or WRITE. To drive full throughput with 4 MB messages, TCP used over 20% of CPU cycles across all cores; the RDMA client used under 3% and the server almost none.

blocks.title: User-level latency of a 2 KB transfer (40 Gbps, unloaded)

scenes.caption: Measured averages from the DCQCN paper. TCP is about 15x slower than a one-sided RDMA operation for the same 2 KB.
SEND is slower than READ or WRITE because the receiver's NIC must also match the message to a posted receive buffer and report it. Lesson 4 explains these operations.

blocks.md: RDMA is not "the OS is gone". The kernel driver still creates queues, pins and maps memory, and handles errors. What disappears is per-message kernel work. That split between a slow **control path** and a fast **data path** is the design of the whole API.

blocks.prompt: Client A issues an RDMA READ of 2 KB from server B's memory. How much CPU work does server B's processor do for this request?
blocks.reveal: Essentially none. The NVIDIA manual says RDMA reads are performed *with no notification whatsoever* to the remote host, and the DCQCN measurements show the RDMA server consuming almost no CPU. NIC B looks up the memory registration, DMAs the bytes out of RAM and sends them back. B's application learns nothing unless the protocol tells it. That is the power of RDMA, and also (as later lessons show) its main programming difficulty.

blocks.question: You already use `sendfile` so the server never copies file bytes into user space. Which cost does RDMA remove that `sendfile` still pays?
options: Running the transport protocol and a system call on the host CPU for each message
The copy from the page cache into a socket buffer
The DMA from host memory to the NIC
The need to know the destination address
blocks.explain: `sendfile` already avoids the user-space copy, and DMA between memory and the NIC happens in both designs. What stays with sockets is the kernel: a system call per operation and the TCP stack running on a CPU per packet. RDMA moves the transport into the NIC and lets the application post work without entering the kernel.

blocks.question: In an RDMA Reliable Connection, which component retransmits a lost packet?
options: The application, after a timeout
The kernel TCP stack on the sender
The sender's NIC hardware
The network switch
blocks.explain: The NIC implements the transport. For RC the hardware tracks packet sequence numbers and acknowledgements and retries on timeout; only when retries are exhausted does the application see an error completion. There is no TCP stack involved in InfiniBand or RoCE.

lessons.title: Queue pairs, work requests and the completion queue

blocks.md:
Applications talk to an RDMA NIC through the **verbs** API, implemented on Linux by `libibverbs` in the rdma-core project. Three objects carry all traffic:

- **Queue pair (QP)**: a send queue plus a receive queue. The manual calls it roughly equivalent to a socket.
- **Work request (WR)**: one operation you post, such as "send these 64 bytes". `ibv_post_send` posts to the send queue, `ibv_post_recv` to the receive queue.
- **Completion queue (CQ)**: a FIFO of **completion queue entries (CQEs)**, one per finished WR, successful or not. Many QPs may share one CQ.

Posting does not enter the kernel. The library writes a **work queue element (WQE)**, the NIC's own format of your WR, into a ring buffer in host memory, then writes to a NIC register mapped into the process (an MMIO write called a **doorbell**). The NIC fetches the WQE by DMA, executes it, and DMAs a CQE into the CQ. `ibv_poll_cq` just reads that memory: polling is a function call, not a system call.

blocks.caption: Post one signaled SEND and spin until its completion arrives (setup and error handling elided).

blocks.title: One SEND from post to completion

scenes.caption: The scatter/gather entry names local memory by address, length and the lkey from its registration (lesson 3).
wr_id is your own tag. The NIC never interprets it; it is copied into the matching completion so you know which request finished.
ibv_post_send writes a WQE into the send ring and rings the doorbell. It returns as soon as the WQE is queued, long before the bytes leave.
Busy-poll the CQ. ibv_poll_cq returns 0 while nothing has completed, so this loop spins in user space.
The NIC has the remote acknowledgement and DMAs a CQE. Poll returns 1 and wc carries our wr_id and status.
Only after the completion is it safe to overwrite buf. Before this point the NIC may still be reading it by DMA.

blocks.md: The rdma-core man page is explicit: buffers used by a WR may only be reused after the request completes and its completion has been polled. The one exception is `IBV_SEND_INLINE` (SEND and RDMA WRITE only), which copies the payload into the WQE itself, so the buffer is reusable as soon as `ibv_post_send` returns.

A completion costs the NIC a DMA write and costs you a poll. If the QP is created with `sq_sig_all = 0`, only WRs with `IBV_SEND_SIGNALED` produce a send-side CQE. Kalia et al. call the rest **unsignaled**: they generate no CQE, and the application detects their completion by other, application-specific means.

The figure below shows four WRs posted to an 8-slot send queue where only two are signaled.

blocks.title: Send queue and CQ with signaled and unsignaled WRs

scenes.caption: Empty rings. The application owns the producer index of the send queue; the NIC owns the consumer side.
Post WRs 1 to 4 in one call (a linked list). WR 2 and WR 4 are signaled, WR 1 and WR 3 are not. One doorbell covers all four.
The NIC executes WR 1 and WR 2 in order. Only WR 2 produces a CQE.
All four done, two CQEs. A send queue completes in order, so the CQE for wr2 also tells you wr1 has finished. The usual rule: free unsignaled slots and buffers when a later signaled WR completes.

blocks.md: Before a QP can carry traffic it walks a state machine with `ibv_modify_qp`: **RESET** to **INIT** to **RTR** (ready to receive) to **RTS** (ready to send). For a Reliable Connection the man page lists the attributes each step needs. RTR is where the QP learns its peer: the remote QP number, the address (an address vector), the path MTU and the starting receive packet sequence number. Those values must reach you out of band, for example over a TCP socket, or by using the `rdma_cm` connection manager library.

blocks.title: Bringing up a Reliable Connection QP

nodes.label:
Peer info (TCP or rdma_cm)
QPN, address, PSN

scenes.caption: A new QP starts in RESET. It can do nothing yet.
INIT sets the port, partition key index and which remote accesses (read, write, atomic) the QP allows. Receives may now be posted but are not processed.
RTR needs the remote side's identity, exchanged out of band: destination QP number, address vector, path MTU, receive PSN, plus RC limits for incoming reads and the RNR timer.
RTS adds the send PSN, the ACK timeout and the retry counts. Only now can ibv_post_send run. Lesson 6 shows what those timeouts mean.

blocks.question: This code posts a signaled SEND of `buf`, then immediately does `memcpy(buf, next_msg, 64)` and posts another SEND of `buf`, and only then polls the CQ. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: ibv_post_send copies the payload before it returns
The first message may go out containing bytes of next_msg, because the NIC may still be reading buf
The second post fails because only one WR may be outstanding
The CQ will overflow after two posts
blocks.explain: Posting only queues a WQE that points at buf; the NIC reads the payload later by DMA. Overwriting buf before the first completion is a race. Either wait for the completion, use a second buffer, or (for small payloads) set IBV_SEND_INLINE so the data is copied into the WQE at post time.

blocks.question: A program posts receive buffers and sends but never calls `ibv_poll_cq` on a busy CQ. What happens according to the verbs documentation?
options: Old CQEs are silently overwritten and traffic continues
The NIC stops sending until the CQ has room, like TCP flow control
The kernel enlarges the CQ automatically
The CQ overruns: IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR is raised and the CQ can no longer be used
blocks.explain: The ibv_poll_cq man page warns that you must consume completions fast enough to avoid overrun; an overrun triggers IBV_EVENT_CQ_ERR and the CQ becomes unusable, and the manual adds that its QPs get a fatal event. Size the CQ for the maximum number of outstanding signaled WRs and receives.

blocks.question: Your QP is in RTR. Which is true?
options: It can process incoming messages but cannot yet post sends
It can post sends but not receive
It can do both; RTS only enables atomics
It cannot do anything until RTS
blocks.explain: RTR means ready to receive: receive processing starts at RTR. The transition to RTS adds the send-side parameters (send PSN, timeout, retry counts), after which ibv_post_send works.

lessons.title: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys

blocks.md:
A NIC moves data with DMA, which uses physical (bus) addresses. Your program only knows virtual addresses, and the kernel is free to swap a page out or move it. If the NIC is to write into your buffer without asking the kernel each time, three things must be settled in advance: the pages must stay put, the NIC must know where they are, and somebody must decide who may touch them.

That is **memory registration**. The NVIDIA manual describes it: registration *pins* the pages (no swapping, fixed virtual-to-physical mapping), the OS checks permissions, and the virtual-to-physical table is written to the network adapter.

blocks.caption: Register 1 MiB for local writes and remote read and write. The returned MR carries the two keys.

blocks.md:
`ibv_reg_mr` returns an MR with two keys:

- **lkey**: goes in `ibv_sge.lkey` of your own WRs, so the local NIC knows the buffer is registered.
- **rkey**: you send it, together with the buffer's address, to a peer. The peer puts both into `wr.rdma.remote_addr` and `wr.rdma.rkey` of its RDMA READ, WRITE or atomic.

A **protection domain (PD)** groups objects that may work together: a QP can only use MRs from its own PD. Access flags are checked too. If you ask for `IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_WRITE` or `IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_ATOMIC`, the man page requires `IBV_ACCESS_LOCAL_WRITE` as well; local read is always enabled.

Concrete example. A buffer of 8 pages (4 KB each) starts at virtual address `0x10000`. A peer issues an RDMA WRITE of 64 bytes to `remote_addr = 0x12100` with our rkey. The NIC checks the rkey and the bounds, then computes the offset `0x12100 - 0x10000 = 0x2100 = 8448` bytes. That is page $8448 / 4096 = 2$ (rounded down) at offset $8448 - 2 \cdot 4096 = 256$, and the NIC writes to that page's physical frame plus 256.

scenes.caption: Before registration: 8 virtual pages (hex addresses). Their physical frames are known only to the kernel and could change at any time.
ibv_reg_mr pins all 8 pages and writes their frame numbers into the NIC's translation table (frame numbers here are illustrative). The MR now has an lkey and an rkey.
An RDMA WRITE arrives for 0x12100. Offset 0x2100 = 8448 bytes, so page index 2, byte 256. The NIC DMAs 64 bytes into frame c19 at offset 256. No host CPU is involved.
A WRITE to 0x18000 is past the end of the 32 KB region. The NIC rejects it and the requester gets a remote access error completion. Bounds are enforced in hardware.

blocks.md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

The NIC cannot hold unlimited translations. The FaRM paper (Microsoft, NSDI 2014) reports that its NICs keep page tables in system memory and use on-NIC memory as a cache, so a miss costs a fetch across PCIe. With ordinary pages, their 64-byte RDMA read rate dropped by a factor of 4 once more than 16 MB was registered. FaRM's fix was a kernel driver (PhyCo) allocating physically contiguous 2 GB regions so the NIC could use 2 GB pages.

blocks.caption: FaRM's "more than half a million" entries per region dropped to one. 16 MB at 4 KB pages is already 4096 entries.

blocks.title: Translation entries the NIC must cache

scenes.caption: For one 2 GiB region: half a million entries with 4 KiB pages, 1024 with 2 MiB huge pages, 1 with 2 GiB pages.
FaRM registered up to 100 GiB. With 4 KiB pages that is 26.2 million entries, hopeless for an on-NIC cache; with 2 GiB pages it is 50.

blocks.md: Registration is control-path work: a call into the kernel that walks, pins and maps every page. Systems therefore register big pools up front and carve buffers out of them instead of registering per message. Two newer variants from the same man page are worth knowing: `IBV_ACCESS_ON_DEMAND` creates an on-demand paging MR whose pages need not be pinned in advance, and `ibv_reg_dmabuf_mr` registers memory exported as a dma-buf, which is how device memory such as a GPU's can be registered. NVIDIA's GPUDirect RDMA uses PCI Express peer-to-peer transfers so the NIC reads and writes GPU memory directly.

blocks.question: A peer's RDMA WRITE targets `remote_addr = 0x15040` in the 8-page region starting at `0x10000` (4 KB pages). Which page index and byte offset does the NIC write?
options: Page 4, offset 0x40
Page 5, offset 0x400
Page 5, offset 64
Page 21, offset 64
blocks.explain: Offset = 0x15040 - 0x10000 = 0x5040 = 20544 bytes. 20544 / 4096 = 5 remainder 64. So page index 5 at byte 64 (0x40). Page 21 comes from forgetting to subtract the base.

blocks.question: `ibv_reg_mr(pd, buf, len, IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_WRITE)` returns NULL. Most likely cause?
options: Remote write requires IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_READ
The buffer must be registered by the peer, not locally
Remote write is only allowed on UD QPs
Remote write also requires IBV_ACCESS_LOCAL_WRITE
blocks.explain: The ibv_reg_mr man page states that if IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_WRITE or IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_ATOMIC is set, IBV_ACCESS_LOCAL_WRITE must be set too. Remote read is independent, and UD QPs do not support RDMA WRITE at all.

blocks.question: A cache server registers each 4 KB request buffer just before using it and deregisters it after. Throughput is poor. What is the best fix?
options: Use RDMA READ instead of WRITE
Register one large pool at startup, preferably on huge pages, and reuse buffers from it
Disable the protection domain
Use more QPs
blocks.explain: Registration enters the kernel and pins pages, so per-request registration puts the slow control path back on the data path. Registering a pool once fixes that, and large pages keep the NIC's translation cache small (FaRM's lesson).

lessons.title: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics

blocks.md:
Verbs come in two families (Kalia et al. call them messaging verbs and memory verbs):

- **Two-sided**: SEND on one side consumes a RECEIVE posted earlier on the other. The receiver's CPU decides where data lands by posting buffers, and it gets a completion.
- **One-sided**: RDMA WRITE, RDMA READ and atomics name a remote address plus rkey. The remote NIC executes them against registered memory and the remote CPU is not told.

The sequence below runs all three on a Reliable Connection.

blocks.title: SEND, WRITE and READ on one RC connection

scenes.caption: Two-sided needs preparation: App B posts a receive buffer first. Without it an incoming SEND has nowhere to go.
A posts a SEND. NIC B places the payload in the next posted buffer, acknowledges, and both sides get a completion.
RDMA WRITE carries remote_addr and rkey. NIC B writes memory and acknowledges. App B is never notified.
RDMA READ: NIC B reads the bytes from registered memory and returns them. Again B's CPU is untouched; only A gets a completion.

blocks.md:
If a SEND (or a WRITE with immediate) arrives on an RC QP and no receive is posted, the responder returns **Receiver Not Ready (RNR)**. The sender's NIC waits and retries up to `rnr_retry` times (the value 7 means retry forever); if that runs out, the WR completes with `IBV_WC_RNR_RETRY_EXC_ERR`. Keeping enough receives posted is the receiver's job.

The transport you pick limits which verbs exist (rdma-core `ibv_post_send` man page and NVIDIA manual):

- **RC** (Reliable Connected): SEND, WRITE, READ, atomics. One QP talks to exactly one remote QP, in order and acknowledged, much like TCP. Messages up to 1 GB.
- **UC** (Unreliable Connected): SEND and WRITE, no READ or atomics, no retransmission.
- **UD** (Unreliable Datagram): SEND only, each message at most one MTU, but one QP can reach any other UD QP, much like UDP.

blocks.prompt: App B must react when App A's RDMA WRITE lands, but a plain WRITE produces no completion on B. How can B find out?
blocks.reveal:
Two common answers:

1. **WRITE with immediate**: the data is placed as usual, and a 4-byte immediate value is delivered in a completion on B. It consumes one posted receive, just like a SEND.
2. **Poll memory**: B's CPU repeatedly reads a word in the target buffer until it changes. This is how FaRM implements messaging, shown next. It avoids receive posting entirely but costs a polling core and depends on the order in which the NIC writes bytes.

blocks.md: FaRM builds a message channel out of RDMA WRITEs into a ring buffer that lives on the receiver, one ring per sender and receiver pair. Free space is kept zeroed. The receiver polls the word at its head: a non-zero value L means a message of length L has started, and it then polls the message trailer to know the whole message has arrived. The sender keeps a lagging copy of the receiver's head, which the receiver refreshes with an RDMA WRITE only after processing at least half the buffer, so the sender never overwrites unprocessed data.

blocks.title: FaRM-style ring: messages by RDMA WRITE plus polling

scenes.caption: Simplified 12-slot ring, all zero. The receiver polls slot 0 (its head). The sender writes at its tail, also slot 0.
Sender issues one RDMA WRITE: length 3, three payload words, then a trailer marker. The receiver CPU was not involved in placing it.
Receiver sees a non-zero head, polls the trailer at slot 4, then processes the message and zeroes the slots so they read as free again.
A second message lands at slot 5. The sender's copy of head still says 0 (it lags), which is safe: it only limits how far ahead the sender may write.

blocks.md: Polling the trailer only works if the NIC writes the message in increasing address order. FaRM notes that many NICs, including theirs, guarantee this for RDMA writes but not reads. It is a hardware property, not a verbs promise: registering memory with `IBV_ACCESS_RELAXED_ORDERING` explicitly gives up write-after-write ordering.

**Atomics** (RC only) are fetch-and-add and compare-and-swap on a remote 8-byte word: the NIC returns the old value. They look like a perfect distributed counter, but Kalia et al. (USENIX ATC 2016) found NICs implement them with internal locks and a read-modify-write over PCIe. On ConnectX-3 total atomic throughput stayed at 2.7 million ops/s regardless of how many counters were used. A sequencer built on fetch-and-add reached 2.24 million requests/s, while their RPC-based sequencer, where a server CPU increments the counter, reached 122 million.

blocks.title: Networked sequencer throughput (Kalia et al., Connect-IB)

scenes.caption: One-sided atomics bypass the server CPU, yet lose: every request contends for the same NIC-internal lock on one counter.
The best design is about 54x faster. The CPU can batch increments in its cache; the NIC cannot. One-sided is not automatically fastest.

blocks.question: You want one server to accept requests from 10,000 clients with as little NIC state as possible. Which transport fits, and what does it give up?
options: UD: one QP can talk to every client, but only SEND/RECV of at most one MTU per message
RC: it supports every verb
UC: it is unreliable, so it needs no state
UD: it supports RDMA READ without connections
blocks.explain: A connected QP (RC or UC) talks to exactly one peer, so 10,000 clients need 10,000 QPs. A UD QP can exchange datagrams with any UD QP, which is why designs like HERD use it for responses. The price: no RDMA READ/WRITE or atomics, no reliability, and single-MTU messages.

blocks.question: A key-value store uses RDMA WRITE (no immediate) for requests into a server buffer. The server's CPU never notices new requests. Why?
options: WRITE requires an RNR retry first
A plain RDMA WRITE generates no completion or notification on the responder; the server must poll memory or the client must use WRITE with immediate
The rkey is wrong
WRITE only works on UD
blocks.explain: One-sided WRITE is invisible to the responder's CPU by design. Either poll a flag or length word in the buffer (FaRM style, relying on in-order placement) or use WRITE with immediate, which consumes a posted receive and produces a CQE.

blocks.question: Why did the fetch-and-add sequencer lose to an RPC design even though it never touches the server CPU?
options: Atomics are not supported on RC
All requests serialize on a lock inside the NIC, held for a PCIe round trip each
Atomics use UD and drop packets
The CPU is interrupted for each atomic
blocks.explain: Kalia et al. explain that NIC processing units take an internal lock for the target address and do a read-modify-write over PCIe, holding it for hundreds of nanoseconds. One hot counter turns into a serial queue.

lessons.title: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets

blocks.md:
All three RDMA networks expose the same verbs API; they differ below it.

- **InfiniBand (IB)**: its own switches, link and network layers. The link layer uses hop-by-hop credit-based flow control so switches never drop packets for lack of buffer, and a **subnet manager** assigns addresses (LIDs) and computes routes.
- **RoCEv2** (RDMA over Converged Ethernet): keeps the IB transport, but carries it in UDP over IP over Ethernet. The Linux kernel defines its UDP destination port as 4791. The IP header allows routing; the UDP header lets switches spread flows across paths with ECMP hashing.
- **iWARP**: an IETF stack. RDMAP (RFC 5040) runs on DDP (RFC 5041), which runs on MPA framing over TCP. Remote buffers are named by a Steering Tag (STag), the counterpart of an rkey.

scenes.caption: Applications program against verbs. Everything below is chosen by the hardware and network you deploy.
InfiniBand: purpose-built from transport to link. Losslessness comes from credit-based flow control on every link.
RoCEv2: the same IB transport, wrapped in UDP/IP so it runs on routed Ethernet. Ethernet drops when buffers fill, so deployments add Priority Flow Control to make it lossless.
iWARP: reliability comes from a TCP stack implemented in the NIC, so it tolerates loss like TCP does, at the cost of TCP's complexity in hardware.

blocks.md:
Why does RoCE care so much about loss? The IB transport was designed for a fabric that does not drop packets, so its recovery is simple. The DCQCN paper notes that ConnectX-3 Pro NICs use **go-back-N**: on a gap in sequence numbers the sender resends everything from the lost packet onward. They measured throughput falling rapidly once the loss rate exceeded 0.1%.

So RoCEv2 is deployed with **Priority-based Flow Control (PFC)**: when a switch ingress queue passes a threshold it sends a PAUSE upstream, and the upstream device stops sending on that link for that priority class (up to eight classes) until resumed. No buffer overflow, no drops.

blocks.title: PFC pauses links, not flows: the victim flow

scenes.caption: Simplified from the DCQCN paper. H1 and H2 (and in the paper, many more senders) send to R through T4. The victim flow VS to VR shares only switch T1 with them.
Incast: T4's queue toward R fills. T4 sends PAUSE to T1 for that priority. T1's queue for the T4 port now grows.
T1's ingress buffers fill, so T1 pauses its upstream ports, including the port VS uses. PAUSE is per port and priority, not per flow.
VS to VR never touches the congested T4, yet its throughput collapses. This is congestion spreading; the DCQCN paper also shows unfair sharing among senders.

blocks.md: The fix in the DCQCN paper is per-flow congestion control so PFC rarely fires. Switches mark packets with ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification, a congestion bit in the IP header) when a queue is long. The receiving NIC (notification point) sends a **Congestion Notification Packet (CNP)** back, at most one per flow every 50 µs in their deployment. The sending NIC (reaction point) cuts its rate using a running estimate of congestion, α:

blocks.caption: On each CNP. R_C is the current rate, R_T the target rate it later recovers toward. With no CNP for K = 55 µs, alpha decays to (1 - g) alpha. The paper uses g = 1/256, and alpha starts at 1.

blocks.title: DCQCN: how hard the next CNP cuts the rate

scenes.caption: Right after congestion alpha is near 1, so a CNP halves the rate. After 256 quiet periods of 55 µs (14.08 ms), alpha is 0.367 and a CNP keeps 81.6% of the rate.
Larger g (here 1/16) forgets congestion much faster, so cuts become gentle within a millisecond. Smaller g reacts more steadily; the paper tunes g with a fluid model.

blocks.md: RoCEv2 gets RDMA onto ordinary routed Ethernet only by making that Ethernet (nearly) lossless with PFC, then taming PFC's side effects with end-to-end congestion control such as DCQCN. Loss is still possible from corruption or misconfiguration, and go-back-N recovery makes it expensive.

blocks.question: Why does RoCEv2 put a UDP header in front of the IB transport header?
options: UDP provides retransmission for RDMA
UDP is required for PFC to work
To make RoCEv2 compatible with iWARP
So routers and switches can hash flows across equal-cost paths (ECMP); IP provides routing
blocks.explain: The DCQCN paper: the IP header is needed for routing, while the UDP header is needed for ECMP. Reliability still comes from the IB transport in the NIC, not from UDP.

blocks.question: In the victim-flow scenario, why is VS to VR slowed even though it never crosses the congested switch?
options: Because PFC pauses a whole port and priority, so every flow behind that port stops
Because ECN marks are broadcast to every flow
Because RoCE has no per-flow sequence numbers
Because DCQCN halves every flow's rate
blocks.explain: PFC is coarse: PAUSE frames apply per port and priority class. Cascading pauses reach ports that carry unrelated flows. Per-flow congestion control (DCQCN) keeps queues short so PAUSE is rarely needed.

blocks.question: A team runs RoCEv2 on a network that drops 1% of packets and sees awful throughput. Given go-back-N in the NIC, what is the best first move?
options: Increase message size so fewer messages are sent
Make the fabric lossless for RDMA traffic (PFC on its priority, ECN-based congestion control) or use a transport that recovers loss better
Switch from RC to UC to avoid retransmissions
Raise the ACK timeout
blocks.explain: With go-back-N, each loss resends everything after it, and the paper shows throughput degrading rapidly above 0.1% loss; bigger messages make it worse. UC simply loses data. The fix is to remove loss for RDMA traffic or choose a loss-tolerant transport such as iWARP's TCP.

lessons.title: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure

blocks.md:
RDMA's raw numbers are easy to lose. Kalia et al. measured the best and worst choices of RDMA options differing by 70x in throughput. Three hidden resources usually decide the outcome:

1. **NIC caches**: the NIC caches address translations, QP state and WQEs in on-chip SRAM. Every miss is a read across PCIe.
2. **PCIe transactions**: each doorbell, WQE fetch, payload fetch and CQE write is a PCIe transaction with roughly 20 to 26 bytes of header overhead.
3. **Contention inside the NIC**: operations that need cross-QP synchronization, like atomics on one address, serialize.

**QP state.** A connected QP talks to one peer, so the QP count grows with the cluster. FaRM counted QPs per machine for m machines with t threads each: one QP per pair of threads needs $2mt^2$; one QP per thread per remote machine needs $2mt$; sharing a QP among q threads needs $2mt/q$. FaRM measured the best q depends on cluster size: sharing reduces NIC state but costs parallelism and locking.

blocks.title: QPs per machine: 20 machines, 16 threads each

scenes.caption: 2 x 20 x 16 x 16 = 10,240 QPs per machine if every thread connects to every remote thread.
One QP from each thread to each remote machine: 2 x 20 x 16 = 640.
Four threads share each QP: 640 / 4 = 160. Less QP state to cache, more contention per QP. UD avoids per-peer QPs entirely, at UD's limits.

blocks.md: **Doorbells and WQE size.** There are two ways to hand WQEs to the NIC. With *WQE-by-MMIO* the CPU writes the whole WQE into the NIC's mapped memory, in 64-byte write-combined chunks. With a *Doorbell* the CPU writes a small doorbell and the NIC fetches the WQEs by DMA. If you post several WRs at once, one doorbell covers the batch (**Doorbell batching**). For 10 WQEs of 65 bytes on PCIe 3.0, Kalia et al. compute 1800 bytes of PCIe traffic with WQE-by-MMIO versus 1534 with one doorbell, and 20 MMIO writes become 1.

blocks.tex: T_{\text{MMIO}} = N \left\lceil \tfrac{D}{64} \right\rceil (64 + P_r) = 10 \cdot 2 \cdot 90 = 1800, \qquad T_{\text{db}} = (d + P_r) + N\,(128 + P_c) = 34 + 1500 = 1534
blocks.caption: N = 10 WQEs of D = 65 bytes, PCIe 3.0 request header P_r = 26 B, completion header P_c = 22 B, doorbell d = 8 B; 65-byte WQEs occupy 128-byte slots. From Kalia et al., Appendix A.

blocks.title: PCIe bytes to hand N WQEs (65 B each) to the NIC

scenes.caption: At D = 65 the doorbell method moves fewer bytes once N is 2 or more, and needs one MMIO instead of 2N. For N = 1 it costs slightly more (184 versus 180 bytes) plus an extra round of latency.

Shrink the WQE to 64 bytes (one cache line): at N = 10, MMIO moves 900 bytes and the doorbell path 784, and the CPU issues 10 MMIOs instead of 1. Simplified: extends the paper's PCIe model to other sizes; real NICs also differ in DMA and MMIO throughput.

blocks.md: Related tricks from the same paper: **inline** small payloads in the WQE (saves the NIC a DMA read of the payload; on Mellanox NICs an RC WRITE WQE is a 36-byte header plus the inlined bytes, so 28 bytes of payload still fit in one 64-byte cache line), use **unsignaled** WRs to skip CQE writes, and keep WQEs to as few cache lines as possible: shrinking a WQE from 129 to 128 bytes cuts MMIOs from 3 to 2.

**Timeouts and failure.** On an RC QP, the `timeout` attribute set at RTS is an exponent: the Linux kernel documents the ACK timeout as $4.096 \cdot 2^{\text{timeout}}$ µs. NVIDIA's manual recommends `timeout = 14`, `retry_cnt = 7` and `rnr_retry = 7`. With timeout 14 that is about 67.1 ms per attempt. If the peer never acknowledges and the retries run out, the WR completes with `IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR`, and the QP moves to the error state; the manual's recovery path is to modify it back to RESET or destroy and recreate it. FaRM puts it simply: network failures are exposed as a terminated connection.

blocks.title: Local ACK timeout: 4.096 µs times 2 to the power timeout

scenes.caption: Each step doubles the timeout. timeout = 14 gives 67.1 ms; timeout = 8 gives about 1.05 ms. The value 0 is special: it means wait forever, not 4 µs.
Simplified model: if every attempt times out, a dead peer is detected after roughly (retry_cnt + 1) timeouts, about 537 ms at timeout 14 and retry_cnt 7. Real hardware timing varies.

blocks.md: A short timeout detects dead peers fast but turns a transient congestion spike into a fatal QP error; a long one can stall an application for seconds. Pick it from your fabric's real round-trip and queueing delays, not from habit.

In practice: register big pools on huge pages, keep the number of connected QPs bounded (share, or use UD for fan-out), batch posts behind one doorbell, inline small payloads, signal selectively, avoid hot atomics, and handle error completions by resetting or recreating the connection.

blocks.question: A 64-node cluster with 24 threads per node uses one RC QP between every pair of threads. Using FaRM's formula, how many QPs does each machine hold, and what is the likely symptom?
options: 2 x 64 x 24 = 3072; none, QPs are free
64 x 24 = 1536; the CQ overflows
24 x 24 = 576; RNR errors
2 x 64 x 24 x 24 = 73,728; throughput drops from QP-state cache misses on the NIC
blocks.explain: 2mt squared = 2 x 64 x 576 = 73,728. QP state lives in host memory with the NIC caching it; FaRM saw request rates fall as the cluster grew for exactly this reason. One QP per thread per machine (3072) or sharing among q threads cuts it.

blocks.question: You post 16 small WRITEs per loop iteration, each with its own `ibv_post_send` call. Which change most directly reduces CPU MMIO work?
options: Make every WR signaled
Chain the 16 WRs in one linked list and post them with a single call so one doorbell covers them
Use RDMA READ instead
Increase the CQ size
blocks.explain: ibv_post_send accepts a linked list of WRs. Posting them together lets the driver ring one doorbell and have the NIC fetch all WQEs by DMA (Doorbell batching), instead of one MMIO sequence per WR. Signaling every WR adds CQE writes instead of removing work.

blocks.question: Your RC QP has `timeout = 14` and `retry_cnt = 7`. A peer machine loses power mid-transfer. What does the sender see, and roughly when?
options: Nothing; the WR stays pending forever
An IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR completion after on the order of half a second, with the QP in an error state
An RNR error immediately
A TCP reset
blocks.explain: With no ACKs, the NIC retries after each 67.1 ms timeout; once retry_cnt is exhausted the WR completes with IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR (about 8 x 67 ms = 537 ms in the simple model). RNR is about missing receive buffers on a live peer, not a dead one.
